tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: propose it and call this.

The result says which case below applies. When the box shows your question, it ends your turn: write no text after this call, since the recap and question say what the user needs and your work above holds the detail. Otherwise your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, with any question the box did not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available now, or one your own work this turn made available; anything else is refused, and one that stops being available later is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and the other answers), so do not guess. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Fix 2 instead", "Not now": a button, not a sentence; the detail goes in message. No "@", no leading / or !. Ignored for an app action (the app's own label is used).

message.description: For a reply: what the click sends, up to 300 characters of plain text — no "@" anywhere, no leading / or !. Omit when the label is the whole message.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.description: Run, test, and visually verify iOS apps in the iOS Simulator on this Mac. Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. Simulator only: this tool cannot drive or stream a physical iPhone or iPad. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. If the user wants the app on their real device ("on my iPhone", "on my device"), build and deploy for the device with your normal build tools instead, and say the live panel only shows simulators. 'attach' opens a live panel so the user can watch — when the user wants to see the app, call 'attach' FIRST, before building: it is cheap, opens instantly on a booted simulator, and errors harmlessly when nothing is booted (boot or build, then retry it). 'launch' installs and launches a built .app — build it first, with the user's own build tooling or this server's 'build' tool when this session has it; launch re-attaches on its own, but do not rely on that instead of the early attach. Screenshots and tap/swipe/text verification are headless and need no panel. Don't open the panel when the user only asked to build/compile or to run unit tests. Coordinates are in device points (origin top-left); the 'launch' result reports the device's point dimensions.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

The search results confirm the core requirements, but they don't clearly settle whether the two permissions are separate.

- **User gesture required:** A tutorial says the page must call `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` on iOS 13+, and the permission dialog can only be brought up from a user gesture (tap/click).
- **Already-granted case:** If the user had already granted the permission, you may call requestPermission without an interaction.
- **HTTPS required:** The same tutorial notes that iOS will auto-decline the requestPermission call if the page is not loaded over HTTPS.
- **Orientation API:** A developer forum post shows a separate DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission() call triggered by a button press. It also reports that Safari caches the user's granted or denied answer across page reloads, and that the developer could not find a way to check the existing state.
- **Separate vs. shared:** None of the results say whether granting `DeviceMotionEvent` permission also covers `DeviceOrientationEvent`, or the reverse. The A-Frame docs refer only to DeviceOrientation events, and the tutorial refers to motion. If you need to know whether one grant covers both, you'd need Apple's WebKit documentation or a targeted test on an iOS device.
- **WKWebView:** A WebKit bug thread says the requestPermission() API is only exposed in MobileSafari, not WKWebView.

The search didn't find any source saying Firefox reports `rotationRate` in radians. MDN documents the unit as degrees per second, and it notes that browsers can differ in how they handle these coordinates.

- **Units:** MDN's property page describes `rotationRate` as the device's rotation rate on each axis, in degrees per second. If the hardware can't provide this information, the property returns null.
- **Firefox vs. Chrome:** MDN's DeviceMotionEvent page warns that Firefox and Chrome do not handle the coordinates the same way. It doesn't say what the difference is, and the results don't mention radians.
- **Interval:** MDN describes `interval` as a number representing the interval of time, in milliseconds, at which data is obtained from the device.

Overall, the sources support degrees per second and milliseconds. For the Firefox behavior, you'd need to test on a device or check Firefox's bug tracker.

The search turned up a 2014 W3C public-geolocation mailing list thread that documents this exact discrepancy. I found nothing newer confirming whether iOS Safari still behaves this way.

- **The spec value:** A device lying flat with the screen facing up should report a z value of +9.81 under the spec. The specification says a flat device on a horizontal surface, screen upmost, should have a zero acceleration and an accelerationIncludingGravity z value of 9.81.
- **iOS Safari (as reported in 2014):** In iOS Safari this configuration returned z: -9.81. The same thread notes that the sign is also flipped on the x axis for a vehicle-mounted device.
- **Android Chrome:** Android-based browsers return z: 9.81, which matches the spec.
- **Developer response:** The spec editors and implementers were split on whether to fix this. One maintainer said Chrome for Android is providing the correct values and iOS values are inverted according to the spec guidelines. Another contributor pointed out that browser sniffing to invert values is fragile, since it breaks if either platform changes its behavior.
- **MDN:** The MDN page describes the z axis as running down to up, and says the property returns the acceleration plus the equal and opposite force of gravity, so the spec-aligned sign is the one Android follows.

Practical takeaway: for cross-platform code, normalize the sign yourself. Expect about +9.81 on z for face-up on Android and about -9.81 on iOS, based on these 2014 reports. Check current behavior on real devices before relying on this, because I could not confirm whether Safari has changed since.

- **rotationRate null on iOS:** An Apple Developer Forums thread describes that since iOS 13, `devicemotion` only includes `rotationRate` after the user grants permission through `DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission()`, and it reports null before that. The same thread says `rotationRate` stayed null on iOS 13.4 even after permission was granted, and that the code had worked before the update. - **Axis mismatch:** A 2017 W3C issue notes that Chrome on Android, Firefox on Android, and Safari on iPhone all map the `rotationRate` axes differently from the spec. - **Background tabs / visibilitychange:** I found no source on whether iOS Safari pauses `devicemotion` in background tabs. **Spec mapping:** The devicemotion `rotationRate` section requires the rates to be expressed as the rate of change of the angles defined in section 4.1. Under that definition, alpha maps to the z axis, beta to the x axis, and gamma to the y axis.

**Browser mapping:** Chrome on Android, Firefox on Android, and Safari on iPhone instead map alpha to the x axis, beta to the y axis, and gamma to the z axis.

**Proposed change:** Jun Cai argues that because browsers have shipped the current mapping for some time and all three use it, the specification should be updated to match the implementation rather than the reverse. Jun links a Chromium bug (issue 541607) and a pull request to revise the rotationRate alpha, beta, and gamma description to match the implementation (PR #43).

**GitHub issue:** The discussion is tracked in w3c/deviceorientation issue **#44**.

content.content:
**Shared state:** The controller uses one permission state for both orientation and motion. `m_accessStatePerOrigin` maps each origin (`document.securityOrigin().data()`) to a single `DeviceOrientationOrMotionPermissionState` value, so a decision covers both sensors.

**Already granted or denied:** The prompt is not shown again. In `shouldAllowAccess()`, if `accessState(document)` returns anything other than `Prompt`, the callback runs immediately with that cached value. The chrome client is only asked when the state is `Prompt`. `accessState()` also returns `Denied` when there is no page, and `Prompt` when the top document is in another process. For the top document or a same-origin document, it reuses the top document loader's `deviceOrientationAndMotionAccessState()`.

**User gesture:** The file does not require one. It computes `bool mayPrompt = UserGestureIndicator::processingUserGesture(&document);` and passes that flag to `shouldAllowDeviceOrientationAndMotionAccess()`. The file doesn't show how the client uses it, so the gesture only affects whether a prompt may appear, and that decision happens outside this file.

**Secure context:** This file performs no secure-context check. Any such requirement would have to be enforced elsewhere.

**After a decision:** The result is cached per origin before the callback runs. If the result is `Granted`, the code calls `startListeningForDeviceOrientationIfNecessary()` and `startListeningForDeviceMotionIfNecessary()` on every local frame in the page.

The search results show that Chromium has capped device motion and orientation sensor events at about 60 Hz for years, though they are mostly older code reviews and mailing-list threads, so they may not reflect current behavior.

- **Origin of the 60 Hz target:** A 2014 change raised the device orientation rate to 60 Hz, reportedly to match the requestAnimationFrame rate on most hardware. The change aimed to match requestAnimationFrame rate on most hardware.
- **Sensor frequency hint cap:** A 2016 patch set the cap for the Sensor API: a frequency hint above 60 Hz is reduced to 60 Hz, and negative values raise an exception. Negative frequencies raise an exception, and anything above 60 Hz is capped to 60 Hz.
- **Platform limits:** A later change lowered the rate further where the hardware can't keep up. The effective rate is now the lower of the requested rate, 60 Hz, and the sensor's maximum supported frequency. The frequency is now the minimum of the given frequency and the lesser of the maximum supported frequency and 60 Hz.
- **Unit test:** A unit test checks that the event pump does not deliver events to Blink faster than 60 Hz. It adds a unit test to confirm that events are not delivered to Blink at a rate faster than 60 Hz.
- **Developer demand for higher rates:** Developers have asked for faster rates. A 2016 W3C sensors issue asked for 120 Hz for high-end inertial navigation, and a developer there noted that the roughly 60 Hz limit was not enough for their needs. The Chromium-side replies said the 60 Hz limit is an implementation detail rather than a spec requirement.

**1. accelerationIncludingGravity and the flat-device example**
- The attribute is initialized to null and "represents the device's acceleration with gravity." (Quote: "represents the device's acceleration with gravity" is about 50 characters.)
- The spec says that when acceleration includes gravity, the value reflects gravity's effect as proper acceleration.
- For a device lying flat with the screen facing up, the spec gives `acceleration` as zero and `accelerationIncludingGravity` as `{x: 0, y: 0, z: 9.8}`. So the z value is 9.8.

**2. rotationRate units and axes**
- Units are degrees per second (deg/s).
- The device frame has x in the screen or keyboard plane, positive toward the right side. y is in the same plane, positive toward the top. z is perpendicular to the screen, positive out of it.
- Rotations follow the right-hand convention.
- For the orientation angles, alpha rotates about z, beta about x′, and gamma about y″, applied in that order (Z–X′–Y″ Tait-Bryan angles).
- Note: the `rotationRate` IDL getters map alpha to the x-axis rate, beta to y, and gamma to z. That differs from the orientation-angle naming, so check it when reading rotation rates.

**3. interval**
- It is the interval at which data is obtained from the underlying hardware.
- It is expressed in milliseconds (ms).
- It is constant, which the spec says simplifies filtering by the web application.

**4. requestPermission() methods**
- `DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission(absolute = false)` and `DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission()` both exist as static methods.
- Both return `Promise<PermissionState>`.
- User activation: if a required permission is still in the "prompt" state and the page has no transient activation, the promise rejects with a NotAllowedError. So activation is needed only when a prompt would appear.
- Secure context: all these interfaces and the event handler attributes are marked [SecureContext].
- Permissions: they are not separate. Both use the "accelerometer" and "gyroscope" permissions. The orientation method adds "magnetometer" when `absolute` is true. The spec notes there is no algorithm for requesting several permissions at once.

**5. Visibility and background behavior**
- The orientation and motion algorithms return without firing if the document's visibility state is not "visible."
- The security section also says implementations must fire events only when the active document's visibility state is "visible."

**6. Null values**
- `DeviceMotionEvent.acceleration`, `accelerationIncludingGravity`, and `rotationRate` are nullable, and each is initialized to null.
- Their x, y, and z members (or alpha, beta, and gamma for rotationRate) are nullable and are set to null when a value "cannot be provided."
- If the implementation can never provide motion information, the event fires with those attributes set to null.
- Similarly, `alpha`, `beta`, and `gamma` on `DeviceOrientationEvent` may be null, and are null if orientation can never be provided.

The search confirms the core behavior: on iOS Safari, `alpha` is not a compass heading, and `webkitCompassHeading` is the compass-based value.

- **webkitCompassHeading.** The caniuse-derived description says Safari instead offers webkitCompassHeading, which has the opposite sign to alpha and is also relative to magnetic north instead of true north. **Acceleration (accelerationIncludingGravity):** The gyro path computes total acceleration as user acceleration plus gravity, per axis: "totalAccel.x = userAccel.x + gravity.x;". It then scales by `kGravity`, defined as "static const double kGravity = 9.80665;". Both the user and total values are multiplied by `kGravity` and passed without negation. The accelerometer-only fallback scales the raw reading the same way: "accel.x * kGravity, accel.y * kGravity, accel.z * kGravity".

**Rotation rate:** The code reads `CMRotationRate rotationRate = newMotion.rotationRate;` and passes it as "rad2deg(rotationRate.x), rad2deg(rotationRate.y), rad2deg(rotationRate.z)". So the values are converted from radians to degrees, and x, y, z are passed in that order. This file does not name them alpha, beta, or gamma. The event construction happens in `motionChanged` in another file, which isn't shown.

**Update interval:** `kMotionUpdateInterval` is referenced but not defined in this file. It is applied with "[m_motionManager setDeviceMotionUpdateInterval:kMotionUpdateInterval];" (or the accelerometer equivalent) and also used for the update timer. The interval is not passed to the event; the `motionChanged` calls contain no interval argument.

**Gyroscope check:** Yes. In `update`, the code uses "if (m_gyroAvailable && deviceMotion)" to choose the gyro path. Otherwise it falls back to accelerometer data. The accelerometer path passes "std::nullopt, std::nullopt, std::nullopt" for the rotation values, so they are null when there is no gyroscope.

**`requestPermission` (Apple WebKit, BSD-licensed; excerpts are short and attributed to Apple Inc.)**

The function checks conditions in this order:

1. **No page or window:** `if (!window || !document.page())` rejects with `InvalidStateError`, message `"No browsing context"`.
2. **Device motion not allowed:** `if (!window->isAllowedToUseDeviceMotion(errorMessage))` logs a console warning, `makeString("Call to requestPermission() failed, reason: "_s, errorMessage, '.')`, at `MessageLevel::Warning` from `MessageSource::JS`. It then resolves with `promise.resolve(PermissionState::Denied)`.
3. **Access controller:** `protect(protect(document.page())->deviceOrientationAndMotionAccessController())->shouldAllowAccess(` is called with the document and a callback.
4. **Prompt state:** If `permissionState == PermissionState::Prompt`, it rejects with `NotAllowedError` and the message `"Requesting device motion access requires a user gesture to prompt"`.
5. **Otherwise:** it resolves with the returned `permissionState`.

The code does not contain explicit checks for a secure context or for feature policy. Those cases may be handled inside `isAllowedToUseDeviceMotion` or the controller, but this file doesn't show it. The "no user gesture" case is not checked directly here. It surfaces as the `Prompt` state from `shouldAllowAccess`, which rejects with the message above.

**Getters (`acceleration()`, `rotationRate()`)**

There are no `canProvide` checks in this file. Each getter fetches the pointer from the internal data and passes it to a static `convert` helper:

- `auto* acceleration = m_deviceMotionData->acceleration();` followed by `return convert(acceleration);`
- The helper returns `std::nullopt` for a null input: `if (!acceleration) return std::nullopt;`. `rotationRate()` follows the same pattern.

On the write path, `initDeviceMotionEvent` uses a separate `convert` overload. It returns `nullptr` when every component is zero, for example `if (!acceleration->x && !acceleration->y && !acceleration->z) return nullptr;`.

{ x: 0, y: 0, z: 9.8 }

To block those, it suggests `overscroll-behavior-x: none`, but notes that this is "still being implemented" in Chrome. It also says that applying `contain` to `html` "prevents overscroll navigation actions."

**Issue #44** in w3c/deviceorientation (opened Aug 23, 2017 by juncaidf) reported that `devicemotion.rotationRate` axis mapping didn't match the spec.

- **Spec:** The spec says rotationRate "must be expressed as the rate of change of the angles defined in section 4.1." The reporter read this as alpha = z axis, beta = x axis, gamma = y axis.
- **Browsers tested:** Chrome on Android, Firefox on Android, and Safari on iPhone. All mapped alpha to the x axis, beta to the y axis, and gamma to the z axis.
- **Proposed fix:** The reporter suggested updating the spec to match the browsers, via PR #43.

**Resolution:**
- andybloch argued that the implementations should be fixed instead, since "I don't think it's a good idea to break a specification to match a broken implementation." They also suggested renaming or deprecating the old names as an option.
- reillyeon supported updating the spec because the browsers already agreed on the behavior, creating a "defacto standard." He also noted that a Chrome change had been approved on blink-dev, though andybloch pointed out that thread covered units (radians/sec vs. degrees/sec), not axes.
- PR #43 was merged on Jan 31, 2019, and reillyeon closed the issue as completed.

The issue thread doesn't show the final wording of PR #43, so I can't confirm the exact text that was adopted.

The search didn't turn up a source that states the CoreMotion sign for a face-up device, so the z = -1 expectation is unconfirmed here.

- **Relationship to userAcceleration:** Apple's documentation says the device's total acceleration is the sum of gravity and user acceleration, and that the accelerometer measures the sum of two acceleration vectors: gravity and user acceleration. The gravity vector is expressed in the device's reference frame.
- **Units:** A forum thread reports that CMDeviceMotion returns linear acceleration and gravity vector in units of "G"s. The same thread notes that a test found gravity magnitude is equal to 1.0, which fits a gravity vector of about (0, 0, ±1) when lying flat.
- **Sign convention:** I found no Apple text stating the sign of gravity's z component. The W3C accelerometer spec says the sign of the acceleration values must be according to the right-hand convention in a local coordinate system, and its device frame has Z-axis ... pointing outwards from the display, and towards the viewer. A W3C mailing-list comment describes the web `accelerationIncludingGravity` reading as the opposite of gravity: for a device lying flat, its z value is +9.8 (the reaction to gravity), not -9.8. That is the opposite sign to the CoreMotion gravity vector you're asking about, so treat the web convention as a contrast, not confirmation.

Bottom line: the sources confirm that gravity + userAcceleration equals total acceleration and that gravity has magnitude about 1 G. They don't confirm the exact sign for a face-up device. Checking this on a device, or in Apple's sample code, would settle it.

# Getting raw accelerometer events

Retrieve data from the onboard accelerometers.

## Discussion

An accelerometer measures changes in velocity along one axis. All iOS devices have a three-axis accelerometer, which delivers acceleration values in each of the three axes shown in the next illustration. The values reported by the accelerometers are measured in increments of the gravitational acceleration, with the value `1.0` representing an acceleration of 9.8 meters per second (per second) in the given direction. Acceleration values may be positive or negative depending on the direction of the acceleration.

![Accelerometers measure changes in velocity along the x, y, and z axes](images/com.apple.coremotion/media-2904020@2x.png)

You access the raw accelerometer data using the classes of the Core Motion framework. Specifically, the [`CMMotionManager`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager) class provides the interfaces for enabling the accelerometer hardware. When enabling the hardware, choose the interfaces that are best suited for your app. You can pull the accelerometer data only when you need it, or you can ask the framework to push updates to your app at regular intervals. Each technique involves different configuration steps and has a different use case.

> Important:
> If your app relies on the presence of accelerometer hardware, configure the `UIRequiredDeviceCapabilities` key of its `Info.plist` file with the `accelerometer` value. For more information about the meaning of this key, see [Information Property List Key Reference](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/General/Reference/InfoPlistKeyReference/).

For information about the coordinate axes of different device types, see [`CMMotionManager`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager).

### Check for the availability of accelerometer data

Accelerometer data might be unavailable for a variety of reasons, so verify that the data is available before you try to obtain it. Check the value of the [`isAccelerometerAvailable`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/isAccelerometerAvailable) property of `CMMotionManager` and make sure it’s `true`. If it’s `false`, starting updates doesn’t deliver any data to your app.

> Important:
> In visionOS, accelerometer data is available only when your app has an open immersive space. For more information, see <doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/SwiftUI/ImmersiveSpace>.

### Get accelerometer data only when you need it

For apps that process accelerometer data on their own schedule, such as games, use the [`startAccelerometerUpdates()`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/startAccelerometerUpdates()) method of [`CMMotionManager`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager) to start the delivery of accelerometer data. When you call this method, the system enables the accelerometer hardware and begins updating the [`accelerometerData`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/accelerometerData) property of your [`CMMotionManager`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager) object. However, the system does not notify you when it updates that property. You must explicitly check the value of the property when you need the accelerometer data.

Before you start the delivery of accelerometer updates, specify an update frequency by assigning a value to the [`accelerometerUpdateInterval`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/accelerometerUpdateInterval) property. The maximum frequency at which you can request updates is hardware-dependent but is usually at least 100 Hz. If you request a frequency that is greater than what the hardware supports, Core Motion uses the supported maximum instead.

The example below shows a method that configures accelerometer updates to occur 50 times per second. The method then configures a timer to fetch those updates at the same frequency and do something with the data. You could configure the timer to fire at a lower frequency, but doing so would waste power by causing the hardware to generate more updates than were actually used.

```swift
let motion = CMMotionManager()

func startAccelerometers() {
   // Make sure the accelerometer hardware is available. 
   if self.motion.isAccelerometerAvailable {
      self.motion.accelerometerUpdateInterval = 1.0 / 50.0  // 50 Hz
      self.motion.startAccelerometerUpdates()

      // Configure a timer to fetch the data.
      self.timer = Timer(fire: Date(), interval: (1.0/50.0), 
            repeats: true, block: { (timer) in
         // Get the accelerometer data.
         if let data = self.motion.accelerometerData {
            let x = data.acceleration.x
            let y = data.acceleration.y

### Process a steady stream of accelerometer data

When you want to capture all of the incoming accelerometer data, perhaps so you can analyze it for movement patterns, use the [`startAccelerometerUpdates(to:withHandler:)`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/startAccelerometerUpdates(to:withHandler:)) method of [`CMMotionManager`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager). This method pushes each new set of accelerometer values to your app by executing your handler block on the specified queue. The queueing of these blocks ensures that your app receives all of the accelerometer data, even if your app becomes busy and is unable to process updates for a brief period of time.

Before you start the delivery of accelerometer updates, specify an update frequency by assigning a value to the [`accelerometerUpdateInterval`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMMotionManager/accelerometerUpdateInterval) property. The maximum frequency at which you can request updates is hardware-dependent but is usually at least 100 Hz. If you request a frequency that is greater than what the hardware supports, Core Motion uses the supported maximum instead.

The following example shows a method from the [MotionGraphs](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/samplecode/MotionGraphs/Introduction/Intro.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/DTS40012333) sample code project, which you can examine for more context. The app displays a real-time graph of accelerometer data. The user configures the update frequency for the accelerometers using a slider, the changing of which results in a call to the `startUpdatesWithSliderValue:` method shown in the example. This method restarts the accelerometer updates with the new frequency. Each time a new sample is received, the specified block is queued on the main thread. That block updates the app’s graph view and labels with the new accelerometer values.

```objc
static const NSTimeInterval accelerometerMin = 0.01;
- (void)startUpdatesWithSliderValue:(int)sliderValue {
    // Determine the update interval.
    NSTimeInterval delta = 0.005;
    NSTimeInterval updateInterval = accelerometerMin + delta * sliderValue;
    // Create a CMMotionManager object.
    CMMotionManager *mManager = [(APLAppDelegate *)
            [[UIApplication sharedApplication] delegate] sharedManager];
    APLAccelerometerGraphViewController * __weak weakSelf = self;
    // Check whether the accelerometer is available.
    if ([mManager isAccelerometerAvailable] == YES) {
        // Assign the update interval to the motion manager.
        [mManager setAccelerometerUpdateInterval:updateInterval];
        [mManager startAccelerometerUpdatesToQueue:[NSOperationQueue mainQueue]
               withHandler:^(CMAccelerometerData *accelerometerData, NSError *error) {
        [weakSelf.graphView addX:accelerometerData.acceleration.x 
                  y:accelerometerData.acceleration.y 
                  z:accelerometerData.acceleration.z];
        [weakSelf setLabelValueX:accelerometerData.acceleration.x 
                  y:accelerometerData.acceleration.y 
                  z:accelerometerData.acceleration.z];
      }];
   }
   self.updateIntervalLabel.text = [NSString stringWithFormat:@"%f", updateInterval];
}
- (void)stopUpdates {
   CMMotionManager *mManager = [(APLAppDelegate *)
            [[UIApplication sharedApplication] delegate] sharedManager];
   if ([mManager isAccelerometerActive] == YES) {
      [mManager stopAccelerometerUpdates];
   }
}
```

The page says that `preventDefault()` on `touchstart` or the first `touchmove` prevents mouse events, but it doesn't say that it prevents scrolling. The sentences are:

> "Since calling `preventDefault()` on a [`touchstart`] or the first [`touchmove`] event of a series prevents the corresponding mouse events from firing, it's common to call `preventDefault()` on `touchmove` rather than `touchstart`. That way, mouse events can still fire and things like links will continue to work."

From the drawing example:

> "This calls [`event.preventDefault()`] to keep the browser from continuing to process the touch event (this also prevents a mouse event from also being delivered)."

On zooming, the page discusses the second touch:

> "One technique for preventing things like `pinchZoom` on a page is to call `preventDefault()` on the second touch in a series. This behavior is not well defined in the touch events spec and results in different behavior for different browsers (i.e., iOS will prevent zooming but still allow panning with both fingers; Android will allow zooming but not panning; Opera and Firefox currently prevent all panning and zooming.)"

It recommends relying on the meta viewport tag instead of this behavior.

The page doesn't mention passive listeners or `{ passive: false }`. I can't quote a note that isn't there. From general browser behavior (not this page): Chrome and other browsers treat `touchstart` and `touchmove` listeners on the window, document, or body as passive by default, so `preventDefault()` is ignored and logs a console warning. To block the default behavior, register the listener explicitly as non-passive:

```js
canvas.addEventListener("touchmove", handleMove, { passive: false });
```

**Beta and gamma, by source:**

- **Spec (Dec 2011 Working Draft):** beta is rotation around X, range -180 to 180, with 0 at screen-up. Gamma is rotation around Y, range -90 to 90, with 0 at screen-up.
- **iOS Safari:** The author's reading is that beta and gamma are swapped relative to the spec. Beta behaves like a ±90 tilt with 0 at screen-up, so it matches the spec's gamma description. Gamma runs from -180 to 180, which matches the spec's beta range. Safari's own documentation reportedly has the two labels swapped too.
- **Chrome/Opera on Android:** Also appear swapped. Beta is 0 at screen-up, +90 with the top edge up, and -90 when inverted. Gamma runs from -90 to 270 rather than the spec's -90 to 90, with -90/270 meaning the screen faces left.
- **Firefox on Android:** The only one the author found matching the spec. Beta runs 0 to -180 and 0 to 180, and gamma runs from 0 to ±90. The author still recommends a gamma range of -180 to 180.

**Which pose gives beta=90:** On Chrome/Opera (and Safari, per the author), beta=+90 is the device standing upright with the screen perpendicular to the ground and the top edge at the top. On Firefox, the author reports -90 for that pose and +90 for the top edge down, so the sign is reversed relative to Chrome and Safari.

**iOS vs. spec for beta/gamma:** iOS does not match. The author reports the axes swapped and the ranges differing from the spec.

**Other fields:** The author also reports that Safari returns `absolute` as undefined, while Chrome, Opera, and Firefox return true.

**accelerationIncludingGravity and rotationRate:** The message doesn't mention either one.

The page doesn't include a paragraph that covers both events together. The relevant text is in two separate sections, "Remove insecure usage of DeviceMotionEvent" and "Remove insecure usage of DeviceOrientationEvent," and they share the same wording:

> "Chromium has been showing deprecation warnings since 2015 whenever the API is used in a non-secure browsing context."

> "Chrome now restricts the API to secure browsing contexts."

Both sections say Chrome now limits these APIs to secure contexts, which removes access on insecure origins. The page doesn't name a milestone for handlers ceasing to fire, and it doesn't say whether handlers are invoked or not on insecure origins. It only says the APIs are restricted and that warnings were shown beginning in 2015.

**touch-action: manipulation:** The post says, "This means WebKit does not consider double-tap gestures on the element, so single taps are dispatched immediately." It also notes, "Note that putting `touch-action: manipulation` on any node opts all children of the node into the fast-tap optimization."

**Double-tap-to-zoom:** The post explains that the delay exists because "we also allow users to double tap to zoom." It adds that WebKit "cannot tell if the user intends on tapping again" after a single tap.

**350ms click delay:** The post opens by stating, "WebKit on iOS has a 350 millisecond delay before single taps activate links or buttons."

**iOS version:** The post does not say which iOS version introduced `touch-action: manipulation`. It only says the feature was implemented in Bug #149854 and is dated December 15, 2015.

# rotationRate

The rotation rate as measured by the device’s gyroscope.

```
var rotationRate: CMRotationRate { get }
```

## Discussion

This property yields a measurement of the device’s rate of rotation around three axes. Whereas this property gives the raw data from the gyroscope, the identically named property of [`CMDeviceMotion`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMDeviceMotion) gives a [`CMRotationRate`](/documentation/CoreMotion/CMRotationRate) structure measuring gyroscope data whose bias has been removed by Core Motion algorithms.

The web page content you provided contains only the title, "UIKit | Apple Developer Documentation." It doesn't include any body text, figure captions, or sentences about motion coordinate axes, gyroscope sign convention, or gravity direction, so I can't quote those passages.

From general knowledge of Apple's Core Motion framework (not from the page), these are the conventions to verify against the official Core Motion documentation:

- **Device axes:** The x-axis points to the right side of the device, the y-axis points toward the top edge, and the z-axis points out of the screen toward the user.
- **Gyroscope sign convention:** Rotation rates follow the right-hand rule. A positive rotation about an axis appears counterclockwise when viewed from the positive end of that axis, looking back toward the origin.
- **Gravity at rest:** Core Motion reports gravity as a vector in device coordinates. When the device lies flat face up on a table, gravity is approximately (0, 0, -1) g, so the z-component is about -1. When held upright in portrait, gravity is approximately along -y.

Here is a minimal example that reads these values:

```swift
import CoreMotion

let motion = CMMotionManager()
if motion.isDeviceMotionAvailable {
    motion.deviceMotionUpdateInterval = 1.0 / 60.0
    motion.startDeviceMotionUpdates(to: .main) { data, _ in
        guard let data else { return }
        let g = data.gravity            // unit vector, in g units
        let r = data.rotationRate       // rad/s
        print("gravity:", g.x, g.y, g.z)
        print("rotation rate:", r.x, r.y, r.z)
    }
}
```

**(1) Accelerometer and gravity**

- Formula: The page says "the force of gravity is always influencing the measured acceleration according to the following relationship:", followed by an image. The image's file name gives the formula as A_D = -g - (1/mass)∑F_S. The formula is not in the text itself.
- On a table: "when the device is sitting on a table (and not accelerating), the accelerometer reads a magnitude of g = 9.81 m/s2."
- Free fall: "when the device is in free fall and therefore rapidly accelerating toward the ground at 9.81 m/s2, its accelerometer reads a magnitude of g = 0 m/s2."
- Sign on a flat table: "The stationary device will have an acceleration value of +9.81, which corresponds to the acceleration of the device (0 m/s2 minus the force of gravity, which is -9.81 m/s2)." The z-axis value is +9.81 when the device lies flat in its natural orientation.

**(2) Gyroscope units and sign convention**

- Units: "The gyroscope measures the rate of rotation in rad/s around a device's x, y, and z axis." Table 1 also lists rad/s.
- Sign: "Rotation is positive in the counter-clockwise direction; that is, an observer looking from some positive location on the x, y or z axis at a device positioned on the origin would report positive rotation if the device appeared to be rotating counter clockwise. This is the standard mathematical definition of positive rotation and is not the same as the definition for roll that is used by the orientation sensor."

**(3) Coordinate system**

The page does not state "x right, y up, z out of the screen." It refers to the standard sensor coordinate system only by a link to the overview page. It does give these clues:

- Accelerometer: "If you push the device on the left side (so it moves to the right), the x acceleration value is positive." and "If you push the device on the bottom (so it moves away from you), the y acceleration value is positive."
- Rotation vector reference frame: "X is defined as the vector product Y x Z. It is tangential to the ground at the device's current location and points approximately East." "Y ... points toward the geomagnetic North Pole." "Z points toward the sky and is perpendicular to the ground plane."

# Phone sensors and controller input

Target files: `src/phone/sensorMath.ts`, `src/phone/sensors.ts`, `src/phone/sensorSim.ts`, `src/phone/pads.ts`, `src/phone/pads.css`, `src/phone/wake.ts`, `src/phone/sender.ts`, `src/phone/controller.ts`, `src/phone/sensorMath.test.ts`. Every snippet below was typechecked with the repo's `tsconfig.json` settings (strict, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, bundler resolution, `@shared/*` alias) plus `noUnusedLocals` / `noUnusedParameters`, and the test file passes under the installed vitest 5.0.5 (20 tests). Nothing was written into the repo; the verified copies live in the scratchpad `research/sensors/proj/`.

## 1. The problem, in the words of SPEC.md

- "HTTPS everywhere. iOS only grants motion sensors and the camera on secure pages, and only after a user tap." (section 1). "Browsers: Safari on iOS 16+ and Chrome on Android for phones." "Phone orientation: landscape for Pilot and Gunner. Show a 'rotate your phone' overlay otherwise, since iOS ignores orientation lock." "Keyboard fallback: every role can be played from the scene PC keyboard."
- Lobby: "one big Enable controls button. That single tap is required: it triggers the iOS motion permission and the screen wake lock." (section 2)
- Pilot: "Hold the phone in landscape with both hands, like a steering wheel. Rotate it left or right to steer. Dead zone of 4°, full lock at 35°." "Right thumb holds GAS (the whole right half of the screen). Left thumb holds BRAKE / REVERSE (the left half)." "Calibration: during the countdown the Pilot holds the phone in a comfortable position and taps CALIBRATE. That angle becomes 'straight'." "Phone shows a big steering-wheel graphic that rotates live with the tilt." (section 3)
- Gunner: "turn it left or right to turn the view and the cannon. Gyroscope only: no dragging, no looking up or down." "FIRE: the whole right two-thirds of the screen is one big button. Tap to fire, hold for auto-fire where the weapon allows it." "RECENTER: a smaller button on the left." "Gain of 2 ... A small dead zone (about 2° per second) ignores hand tremor." "Reset: RECENTER snaps the view behind the bow and clears gyro drift." (sections 3 and 4)
- Engineer: "SHAKE TO BAIL ... Shaking empties it." "Portrait or landscape, either works."
- Every controller: "Phones send input 30 times per second, not on every sensor event." "Android vibrates on fire and on hit. iOS Safari has no vibration API, so iOS flashes the screen red instead." "The screen wake lock keeps phones awake for the whole round."
- Protocol (section 11): `PilotIn { steer: number /* -1..1 */, gas, brake }`, `GunnerIn { dYaw: number /* radians since last packet */, fire, recenter }`, `EngIn { use: 0 | 1 | null, shake: number /* 0..1 */ }`.
- Sensor notes (section 11): steering "from the gravity vector in DeviceMotionEvent.accelerationIncludingGravity (the angle of its x and y components, minus the calibration angle). Avoid the alpha, beta and gamma orientation angles: they jump when the phone is held upright, and alpha drifts." Gunner: "read DeviceMotionEvent.rotationRate (the gyroscope, degrees per second) and project it onto the low-pass-filtered gravity vector ... Check the sign on the first test and flip it if left turns right. If rotationRate is null ... fall back to changes in the alpha angle of deviceorientation." Shake: "count peaks where acceleration without gravity exceeds about 15 m/s²." "iOS: DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission() must run inside a tap handler, on HTTPS. One permission covers both steering and gyro aim." "Wake lock: navigator.wakeLock.request('screen') in the same tap."
- Risk table (section 14): "iOS motion permission: Without HTTPS and a user tap, sensors silently return nothing. Test one iPhone through the tunnel during the base phase." Gate 1: "one phone steers a box boat on the TV."

## 2. Decisions and why

| # | Decision | Why | Rejected |
|---|----------|-----|----------|
| D1 | **Steering angle = `atan2(up.x, up.y)` of the low-passed gravity vector, minus the calibrated angle, wrapped to (-180, 180].** | Turning the wheel is a rotation about the screen normal (device z); that rotates the in-plane gravity components by exactly the wheel angle and leaves z alone, so the formula is exact at any constant pitch (checked numerically, section 3). Both landscape orientations just change the calibrated offset (+90 or -90), and the iOS sign inversion shifts both angles by 180, so the difference is unchanged. | `deviceorientation` beta/gamma: Euler angles hit gimbal lock exactly when the phone is upright (beta = 90), which is the pose we use; the spec itself warns about this. `asin(up.y)` (elevation of the long axis): sign flips between the two landscapes and cannot be absorbed by an offset. Raw per-event angles: 60 Hz accelerometer noise of about 0.5 deg peak to peak lands inside the 4 deg dead zone, so a short low-pass (80 ms) is enough. |

### 3.3 What the phone screens draw from the snapshot

- **Pilot wheel**: rotate the wheel SVG by `-snapshot.steerAngleDeg` so its top mark stays pointing at the sky while the phone turns; fill an arc from 0 to `steer` with the dead zone (±4 deg) drawn as a thin grey band and the lock (±35 deg) as end stops. Grey the wheel and show "tilt the phone up" while `steerWeak`, and "tap CALIBRATE" while `!steerCalibrated`. The pilot looks at the wall, so the fill (not the angle) is the part they see in peripheral vision: make it the team colour, 30 vmin tall.
- **Gunner needle**: `yawSinceRecenterRad` is the phone's own estimate of aim versus bow since the last RECENTER; it ignores the sim's aim-assist gain cut (section 4 of the spec, applied in `src/sim`) and the boat's own turning, so treat it as a hint and prefer an `aimRel` field in `Hud` if the contract is extended. Show "no gyroscope, using compass" when `yawSource === 'orientation'`.
- **Engineer**: `shake` drives the bucket animation speed; the water meter comes from `Hud.water`.
- **Debug line** (`describeSensors(snapshot)`): sign in use, yaw source, shake level. Keep it on screen until Gate 1 passes.

## 4. Edge cases and how they are handled

| Case | Behaviour | Handling |
|------|-----------|----------|
| Plain http (LAN IP, no tunnel) | iOS: `requestPermission()` resolves `'denied'` and logs "Call to requestPermission() failed, reason: Browsing context is not secure." Chrome 76+: handlers never fire on insecure origins. | `requestMotionAccess()` checks `window.isSecureContext` first and returns `reason: 'insecure'` with the message "open the https link from the QR". The 1 s watchdog catches anything that slips through. |
| Desktop browser | `DeviceMotionEvent` exists but no events arrive. | Watchdog reports `'no-events'` after 1 s; with `?sim=1` the keyboard source replaces the device. |
| iOS prompt refused | WebKit caches the decision per origin in the UI process; later calls resolve `'denied'` without a prompt, across reloads. | Message tells the player to close the tab, scan again and tap Allow. |
| `requestPermission()` called outside a gesture | Rejects with `NotAllowedError` ("Requesting device motion access requires a user gesture to prompt"). | Mapped to `'needs-gesture'`: "tap Enable controls again". `enableControls()` starts fullscreen, permission and wake lock synchronously before any `await`. |
| Chrome 151+ exposes `requestPermission` | Resolves without a prompt while the default stays ALLOW. | The code calls it whenever it is a function; it is never used as a platform test. |
| `DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission` | WebKit keeps one state for motion and orientation and starts both listeners on grant. | Not called; one prompt. |
| No gyroscope | iOS: `rotationRate === null`. Chrome Android: an object whose `alpha/beta/gamma` are `null` (NaN internally). | `toRot()` returns null for both; `yawSource` becomes `'orientation'` and the heading fallback runs. |
| No linear-acceleration sensor | Chrome Android gives `acceleration` with null fields. | Shake uses `ag - lowpass(ag)`. |
| Tab hidden, screen locked, app switcher | The spec requires events only while the document is visible; timers are throttled; the wake lock is released. | Sender sends one neutral packet and stops; on return it resets the filters (no jump from stale state) and restarts; `WakeLockKeeper` re-requests; the watchdog gives a 1 s grace and then reports `'stalled'` with a "tap to re-enable" button that re-runs `source.start()` (no new prompt: the grant is cached). |
| iOS 16.0 to 16.3 | No `navigator.wakeLock`. | `WakeLockKeeper.supported()` false: show "turn off Auto-Lock in Settings > Display & Brightness for this round". iOS 16.4 to 18.3: works in a Safari tab, not in Home Screen web apps (we use Safari tabs from the camera QR). |
| Phone held flat | In-plane gravity vanishes; `atan2` becomes noise. | `weak` flag: steer holds, wheel greys, CALIBRATE refuses (`calibrateSteer()` returns false). |
| Landscape upside down (angle near ±180) | Wrap boundary. | `wrapDeg` keeps the difference continuous across ±180. |
| Both landscapes, both platforms | Offsets +90/-90 and a 180 shift on iOS. | Absorbed by the calibration difference; verified in `check_math.mjs` for all four combinations at pitch 0, 30, 60. |
| Pilot never taps CALIBRATE | `calibrationDeg` is null. | Steer stays 0 and the wheel shows "tap CALIBRATE"; the host can also broadcast a calibrate during the countdown through the sender's `calibrate` edge. |
| Gyro saturation / glitch samples | Consumer gyros saturate around 2000 deg/s; a glitch would throw the aim. | Rate clamped to ±600 deg/s; `dt` clamped to 100 ms, first sample uses 1/60. |
| Hand tremor and bias drift | Below 2 deg/s. | Soft dead zone removes 2 deg/s without a jump at the edge. |
| Fast swings pollute the gravity estimate | Centripetal acceleration adds to `ag`. | The yaw axis uses a slower filter (0.25 s) and the projection only needs the direction; errors are second order. |
| Aim sign reversed on a phone | Unknown sensor stack. | Persisted "Invert aim" toggle in the gunner screen, plus the sign detector; Gate 1 checklist includes the sign test. |
| `interval` field | iOS 0.01667 (seconds), Chrome 16 (ms). | Never read. |

Without phones (all three of these run from the scene PC):

1. `npm test` runs `src/phone/sensorMath.test.ts`: wrap, dead zone, curve values (19.5 deg -> 0.35, 35 -> 1.0), clockwise 20 deg -> +20 in both landscapes, iOS sign invariance, pitch invariance, weak pose, yaw projection (30 deg/s at a tilted pose, 0 when perpendicular, sign flips with `up`), yaw step (32 deg/s at 1/60 s -> 2 * 30 * pi/180 / 60 rad), 45 deg/s for 1 s -> 2 * 43 deg of view, orientation up vectors, heading continuity across beta = 90, shake peaks (refractory, re-arm, 4 peaks -> 1.0, decay), the sign detector, the low-pass step response, simulator sign conventions, and packet building (a sub-tick FIRE tap still sends `fire: true`).
2. Open `https://localhost:5173/play?room=TEST&sim=1` on the laptop (or the tunnel URL): the keyboard source runs. `A`/`D` roll the wheel (eased to ±35), `W`/`S` pitch, Left/Right arrows turn at 90 deg/s, Space shakes, `I` switches the simulated platform between Android and iOS signs (steer must not change, yaw must not change because the detector and the sign flip cancel), `N` removes the gyroscope (the yaw source switches to orientation and arrows still turn), `L` swaps landscape side (re-calibrate, steer must still be right-positive), `R` resets. With phones (Gate 1, in this order; takes 10 minutes):

| Case | Behaviour | Handling |
|------|-----------|----------|
| Plain http (LAN IP, no tunnel) | iOS: `requestPermission()` resolves `'denied'` and logs "Call to requestPermission() failed, reason: Browsing context is not secure." Chrome 76+: handlers never fire on insecure origins. | `requestMotionAccess()` checks `window.isSecureContext` first and returns `reason: 'insecure'` with the message "open the https link from the QR". The 1 s watchdog catches anything that slips through. |
| Desktop browser | `DeviceMotionEvent` exists but no events arrive. | Watchdog reports `'no-events'` after 1 s; with `?sim=1` the keyboard source replaces the device. |
| iOS prompt refused | WebKit caches the decision per origin in the UI process; later calls resolve `'denied'` without a prompt, across reloads. | Message tells the player to close the tab, scan again and tap Allow. |
| `requestPermission()` called outside a gesture | Rejects with `NotAllowedError` ("Requesting device motion access requires a user gesture to prompt"). | Mapped to `'needs-gesture'`: "tap Enable controls again". `enableControls()` starts fullscreen, permission and wake lock synchronously before any `await`. |

| `DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission` | WebKit keeps one state for motion and orientation and starts both listeners on grant. | Not called; one prompt. |
| No gyroscope | iOS: `rotationRate === null`. Chrome Android: an object whose `alpha/beta/gamma` are `null` (NaN internally). | `toRot()` returns null for both; `yawSource` becomes `'orientation'` and the heading fallback runs. |
| No linear-acceleration sensor | Chrome Android gives `acceleration` with null fields. | Shake uses `ag - lowpass(ag)`. |
| Tab hidden, screen locked, app switcher | The spec requires events only while the document is visible; timers are throttled; the wake lock is released. | Sender sends one neutral packet and stops; on return it resets the filters (no jump from stale state) and restarts; `WakeLockKeeper` re-requests; the watchdog gives a 1 s grace and then reports `'stalled'` with a "tap to re-enable" button that re-runs `source.start()` (no new prompt: the grant is cached). |

All code was typechecked with the repo's strict tsconfig plus noUnusedLocals/Parameters and against the real shared/protocol.ts, shared/state.ts and shared/config.ts now in the repo (InputPacket with seq, EngineerIn, GunnerIn.use for teams of 2, PHONE tunables via tuningFromPhoneConfig(PHONE)); the vitest file passes 20 tests under the installed vitest 5.0.5. Verified copies live in the scratchpad research/sensors/proj/ (nothing was written into the repo; src/phone in the repo is still empty). Three findings change what the task assumed: (1) rotationRate.alpha is the rate about the device x axis (beta y, gamma z) in the current W3C text and in Chromium and WebKit source, not 'alpha about z'; the yaw projection uses (alpha, beta, gamma) as (x, y, z). (2) Chrome shipped DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission in Chrome 151 (Intent to Ship 17 June 2026), so typeof requestPermission === 'function' is no longer an iOS test; the gravity sign is decided by a UA/vendor guess, corrected by a beta-based physics detector in the lobby, with a persisted Invert-aim toggle. (3) event.interval is in seconds on iOS (WebKit passes 1/60 unchanged) and an integer 16 ms on Chrome, so dt comes from performance.now(). Steering is atan2(up.x, up.y) minus the calibrated angle (exact for wheel rotation about the screen normal at any pitch, invariant to landscape side and to the iOS sign flip), yaw is rotationRate dot unit(up) with dead zone 2 deg/s, gain 2 and dYaw accumulated between 30 Hz sends, shake counts peaks above 15 m/s^2 with a 120 ms refractory; all verified by an independent rotation-matrix script and the unit tests.

decisions.decision: Steering angle = atan2(up.x, up.y) of the low-passed (80 ms) gravity vector minus the calibrated angle, wrapped to (-180, 180]; dead zone 4 deg, full lock 35 deg, curve 0.6x + 0.4x^3; hold the last steer and grey the wheel when the in-plane gravity is below 0.35 g.
decisions.rationale: Turning the wheel is a rotation about the screen normal, which rotates the in-plane gravity components by exactly the wheel angle at any constant pitch; both landscape sides only change the calibration offset (+90/-90) and the iOS sign inversion shifts both angles by 180, so the difference is unchanged. Verified with rotation matrices (check_math.mjs) for both platforms, both landscapes, pitch 0/30/60.
decisions.alternatives: deviceorientation beta/gamma (gimbal lock exactly at the upright pose, as the spec warns); asin(up.y) elevation of the long axis (sign flips between the two landscapes, not absorbable by an offset); raw per-event angle without a low-pass.

decisions.decision: Gunner yaw rate = rotationRate . unit(up) with rotationRate = (alpha, beta, gamma) as rates about device x, y, z; soft dead zone 2 deg/s, clamp 600 deg/s, gain 2, dYaw accumulated in radians between sends.
decisions.rationale: Projecting body angular velocity on the world vertical gives the yaw rate at any tilt (checked numerically to 1e-12). The axis mapping alpha=x, beta=y, gamma=z is what the current W3C text, Chromium (RadToDeg(gyro.x,y,z) into Create(alpha,beta,gamma)) and WebKit (rad2deg(rotationRate.x,y,z) into RotationRate::create) all do; the 'alpha about z' reading is the pre-2019 spec that never matched a browser.
decisions.alternatives: rotationRate.alpha or .gamma alone (wrong unless the phone is exactly upright or flat); deviceorientation.alpha deltas as primary (gimbal lock near upright, drift, relative on iOS); Generic Sensor Gyroscope (not in Safari).

decisions.decision: Normalise gravity before projecting: up = sign * accelerationIncludingGravity, sign guessed from UA/vendor (iOS-like => -1), corrected by a GravitySignDetector that votes sign(ag.y) == sign(sin beta) during the portrait lobby (locks after 45 agreeing samples), and a persisted 'Invert aim' toggle (localStorage gr.invertAim) on top.
decisions.rationale: WebKit computes (userAcceleration + gravity) * 9.80665 unnegated from CoreMotion, so iOS reports -9.81 flat face-up while the spec and Chrome report +9.81; an un-normalised projection flips sign on iOS. The detector makes the sign independent of UA sniffing; the toggle is the last resort for an unknown sensor stack.
decisions.alternatives: typeof DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission === 'function' as the iOS test (Chrome 151 ships the same static); 'flip it after the first test' only (18 players bring both platforms).

decisions.decision: dt from performance.now() deltas clamped to [0, 100 ms] (first sample 1/60); event.interval is never read.
decisions.rationale: WebKit passes kMotionUpdateInterval = 1/60 seconds straight into the event; Chromium passes kDefaultPumpDelayMicroseconds / 1000 = 16 (integer ms). Same field, different units.
decisions.alternatives: event.interval with a unit heuristic.

decisions.decision: One ControllerPipeline keeps filtered state; a separate 30 Hz setTimeout loop on an absolute schedule samples it, builds one InputPacket with seq, latches sub-tick FIRE taps so fire=true is sent at least once, reports recenter/use edges once, and on a hidden tab sends one neutral packet, stops, then resets filters and restarts on return.
decisions.rationale: The spec says 30 Hz not per event; 60 Hz events through a tunnel double packets for nothing; sensors stop while hidden (spec) and timers are throttled, so coasting the boat immediately is the safe behaviour; the absolute schedule avoids drift and bursts.
decisions.alternatives: Per-event sends; requestAnimationFrame (throttled in background, tied to display rate); plain setInterval (drifts, bursts after a hiccup).

decisions.decision: Pads use pointer events on one root; a pointer keeps the zone it went down on; touch uses implicit capture, mouse gets setPointerCapture; CSS touch-action: none, user-select: none, -webkit-touch-callout: none, overscroll-behavior: none, 100dvh with 100vh fallback, position: fixed, safe-area padding; plus non-passive touchstart/touchmove/touchend and gesturestart preventDefault and contextmenu cancelled; releaseAll on blur, hidden and pointercancel.
decisions.rationale: Multi-touch and the desktop mouse share one code path; iOS ignores user-scalable=no and WebKit still double-tap-zooms positioned elements with touch-action: none (bug 218015), so the touch-event preventDefaults are needed; overscroll-behavior kills Chrome pull-to-refresh and Safari rubber band; dvh fixes the Safari toolbar.
decisions.alternatives: Touch events only (no mouse for the simulator); zone by current finger position (sliding across the middle flips GAS/BRAKE); click events (350 ms iOS delay, no multi-touch).

decisions.decision: Enable-controls tap starts requestFullscreen (Android), DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission (when present on any platform) and navigator.wakeLock.request synchronously before any await; DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission is not called; a 1 s (PHONE.motionWatchdogSec) watchdog reports no-events/stalled with player-facing messages for insecure, denied, needs-gesture, unsupported.
decisions.rationale: WebKit rejects NotAllowedError without a processing user gesture; one WebKit permission state covers motion and orientation and a grant starts both listeners; on http WebKit resolves denied with 'Browsing context is not secure' and Chrome 76+ never fires, so isSecureContext is checked first and the watchdog catches the rest.
decisions.alternatives: Awaiting the permission before requesting fullscreen (may lose the activation); calling both requestPermission statics (second prompt risk, no benefit).

decisions.decision: WakeLockKeeper re-requests on visibilitychange and tracks the release event; iOS below 16.4 gets a 'turn off Auto-Lock' banner; haptic() uses navigator.vibrate and falls back to a red flash when vibrate is missing or returns false; orientation via screen.orientation.type when present else matchMedia('(orientation: landscape)'); screen.orientation.lock('landscape') attempted after fullscreen on Android only.
decisions.rationale: Browsers release the lock when the page is hidden; wake lock is Safari 16.4+ (full on iOS 18.4, partial 16.4-18.3 not in Home Screen apps); Safari has no vibrate and no lock(); iPhone has no element fullscreen (WebKit 212934 WONTFIX); lib.dom 5.9 declares unlock() but not lock().
decisions.alternatives: NoSleep-style hidden video for iOS 16.0-16.3 (extra asset and autoplay rules).

decisions.decision: Shake = peaks of |linear acceleration| >= 15 m/s^2 with 120 ms refractory and 8 m/s^2 re-arm, counted over a 1 s window, 4 peaks = 1.0; when acceleration is null use ag minus a 0.5 s low-passed gravity.
decisions.rationale: Peaks per second is the spec's definition and is sign-agnostic (magnitude only); Chrome Android can report acceleration with null fields when there is no linear-acceleration sensor.
decisions.alternatives: RMS/energy (slow waving would count as bailing).

decisions.decision: Desktop simulator (KeyboardSensorSource) synthesises devicemotion and deviceorientation samples from a virtual pose with the same frames and the iOS/Android sign switch (I), no-gyro mode (N), landscape side (L); the no-gyro fallback uses the heading of the device aim axis from the full alpha/beta/gamma rotation matrix (continuous across beta = 90) with 360 wrap, and webkitCompassHeading (360 - heading) only when alpha is null.
decisions.rationale: The whole pipeline, not just the UI, runs on a laptop before the first iPhone arrives; a matrix-derived heading does not jump where raw alpha does.
decisions.alternatives: Feeding fake steer values straight into the sender; raw alpha differences.

claims.claim: W3C Device Orientation spec: a device lying flat screen-up has accelerationIncludingGravity {x: 0, y: 0, z: 9.8} (proper acceleration); rotationRate is in deg/s; interval is in ms; acceleration, accelerationIncludingGravity, rotationRate and their fields are nullable; events are fired only while the document is visible.
claims.evidence: WebFetch of https://w3c.github.io/deviceorientation/ (Introduction example, section 3.2 units, section 6.3 nullability, visibility requirement in the algorithms and security section).

claims.claim: In the current spec the rotationRate alpha getter returns the x-axis rotation rate, beta the y-axis, gamma the z-axis; the spec was changed (PR #43, merged 31 Jan 2019, issue #44) to match Chrome Android, Firefox Android and Safari iOS, which all mapped alpha=x, beta=y, gamma=z; the old text implied alpha=z, beta=x, gamma=y.
claims.evidence: Spec section 6.3.2 getter steps; https://github.com/w3c/deviceorientation/issues/44; https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-geolocation/2017Aug/0001.html.

claims.claim: Chromium builds rotationRate as Create(RadToDeg(gyro.x), RadToDeg(gyro.y), RadToDeg(gyro.z)) with signature Create(double alpha, double beta, double gamma); accelerometer readings are passed unnegated; missing sensors give NaN fields whose getters return null; the pump runs at kDefaultPumpFrequencyHz = 60 and reports interval = kDefaultPumpDelayMicroseconds / 1000 (16).
claims.evidence: WebFetch of chromium/chromium raw files device_motion_event_pump.cc, device_motion_event_rotation_rate.h/.cc, device_sensor_event_pump.h. The exact integer 16 is inferred from integer division of 16666 by 1000; unverified on a device.

claims.claim: WebKit iOS computes accelerationIncludingGravity = (userAcceleration + gravity) * 9.80665 from CoreMotion without negation, passes rad2deg(rotationRate.x, y, z) positionally into RotationRate::create(x, y, z), passes std::nullopt rotation when there is no gyroscope, and passes kMotionUpdateInterval = 1.0f/60.0f straight through as the event interval (so event.interval is about 0.0167 seconds on iOS, not ms).
claims.evidence: WebFetch of WebKit raw WebCoreMotionManager.mm, WebCoreMotionManager.h, DeviceMotionClientIOS.mm and DeviceMotionEvent.cpp (interval() returns m_deviceMotionData->interval() unchanged). The seconds value is from source, not measured on a device.

claims.claim: iOS Safari reports z = -9.81 for a flat face-up phone (and y = -9.81 upright) while Android Chrome reports +9.81, i.e. iOS accelerationIncludingGravity points along gravity (down) and Android/spec along the reaction (up).
claims.evidence: Empirical report and Chromium/Opera editor replies on the W3C list (https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-geolocation/2014Nov/0001.html, .../0004.html) plus the WebKit source in sensors-4; Android guide states a stationary device reads +9.81 (https://developer.android.com/develop/sensors-and-location/sensors/sensors_motion). Not re-measured on a current iPhone.

claims.claim: Android gyroscope: rad/s, positive counter-clockwise viewed from a positive position on the axis (right-hand rule); Chrome converts to deg/s. iOS CoreMotion rotationRate is assumed to use the same right-hand convention.
claims.evidence: Android: sensors_motion guide quote. Chrome: RadToDeg in the pump. Apple: the fetched CMRotationRate and CMGyroData pages give no sign sentence, so the iOS sign is inferred from the cross-browser agreement in issue #44 and covered by the invert toggle and the Gate 1 sign test.

claims.claim: WebKit keeps a single DeviceOrientationOrMotionPermissionState per origin (m_accessStatePerOrigin) for both motion and orientation, never prompts again once the state is not Prompt (cached across reloads, UI-process lifetime), passes mayPrompt = UserGestureIndicator::processingUserGesture, and on Granted starts both the orientation and the motion listeners.
